name: TL494IDR
title: TL494 pulse-width-modulation control circuit
summary: A fixed-frequency PWM controller for switching power supplies. One chip holds two error amplifiers, an adjustable sawtooth oscillator set by RT and CT, a dead-time comparator, a pulse-steering flip-flop, a 5 V reference good to 5 %, and two uncommitted output transistors that each sink or source 200 mA. The OUTPUT CTRL pin picks single-ended (both outputs together) or push-pull operation, and the logic keeps either output from pulsing twice in one push-pull cycle. TL494C is rated 0 °C to 70 °C and TL494I -40 °C to 85 °C; TL494IDR is the TL494I in the 16-pin SOIC on a reel.

pins.name: FEEDBACK
pins.function: Feedback node: the joined outputs of both error amplifiers and the control input of the PWM comparator.

pins.name: DTC
pins.function: Dead-time comparator input. Raising it adds off time; 0 V gives the smallest dead time. It must not be left open.

pins.name: CT
pins.function: Timing capacitor to ground; the oscillator ramp appears on it.

pins.name: RT
pins.function: Timing resistor to ground; it sets the charging current of CT.

pins.name: OUTPUT CTRL
pins.function: Mode select: to ground, both outputs switch together (single-ended or parallel); to REF, they alternate (push-pull).

pins.name: REF
pins.function: Output of the internal 5 V reference regulator.

circuits.title: 5 V, 10 A step-down supply: switching and control sections
circuits.description: A single-ended buck converter that turns a 32 V input into 5 V at up to 10 A, switching at 20 kHz. OUTPUT CTRL is grounded, so both output transistors switch together; their drains drive R10 into the base of a PNP driver Q1, which in turn drives the NPN pass transistor Q2 as a hybrid Darlington. Q2 chops the input into the 140 µH inductor with D1 as the freewheel diode. Error amplifier 1 compares half the output (R8, R9) with half the reference (R3, R4), its gain held to about 101 by RF and R5. Error amplifier 2 limits current: R13 in the load return gives 1 V at 10 A against about 1 V from R1 and R2 off REF. RT and CT set the oscillator, and C2 with R6 and R7 on DTC gives a soft start and leaves 0.5 V on DTC in normal running.

circuits.title: 32 V input power source for the 5 V, 10 A supply
circuits.description: The raw DC supply that feeds the buck converter. A 120 V to 24 V, 75 VA transformer drives a 3 A, 50 V full-wave bridge; the rectified output passes through a 0.3 Ω current-limiting resistor into two 20 mF filter capacitors, giving about 32 V DC (34 V peak) at an average 1.6 A.
notes: T1 pins P1 and P2 are the 120 V primary, S1 and S2 the 24 V secondary.

circuits.title: Operational test circuit
circuits.description: The circuit the oscillator, dead-time, PWM-comparator and supply-current figures are measured in. VCC is 15 V; each drain has a 150 Ω, 2 W pull-up to VCC and both sources are grounded. RT is 12 kΩ and CT 0.01 µF. Both non-inverting inputs are grounded and both inverting inputs go through 50 kΩ to REF,; OUTPUT CTRL is tied to REF for push-pull. Test voltages go on DTC and FEEDBACK. Ramping DTC up from 0 V narrows the pulses to zero at its threshold; ramping FEEDBACK up from 0.7 V does the same at the PWM threshold.

operation.text: The TL494 runs at a fixed frequency. CT carries a rising sawtooth, and an output conducts only while that ramp is above both control voltages: the dead-time input and the error-amplifier output on FEEDBACK. A higher control voltage means shorter pulses. In push-pull mode a flip-flop hands successive pulses to the two transistors in turn.

REF is a band-gap 5 V regulator, set to ±5 % initially. It moves less than 25 mV as VCC goes from 7 V to 40 V and less than 100 mV over 0 °C to 70 °C. Besides serving as the reference it powers the output-control logic, flip-flop, oscillator and both comparators. It is short-circuit protected and can supply 10 mA to outside bias circuits.

With VCC under 7 V, REF stays at 0 V until the internal references are valid, then steps up to 5 V, so start-up is predictable. Typical curve: REF is 0 V up to about VCC = 4 V, reaches about 4.5 V at 4.5 V and 5 V by 5 V.

A constant current set by RT charges CT, giving a linear ramp; at 3 V across CT the oscillator discharges it and the cycle starts again. The single-ended output frequency equals the oscillator frequency; in push-pull each output runs at half. The oscillator can be bypassed by tying RT to REF and feeding a sawtooth into CT, or one TL494's oscillator can drive several supplies in step.

The dead-time comparator turns both outputs off whenever DTC is above the ramp. A built-in offset of 110 mV (about 0.1 V) gives a minimum dead time of about 3 % to 5 % with DTC at ground. Taking DTC from 0 V to 3.3 V moves dead time linearly from that minimum to 100 %, which lets outside signals control the duty cycle without touching the error amplifiers. Its input current is under 10 µA. DTC must be driven or tied; left open its state is undefined.

The comparators run from the 5 V reference, isolating them from the input supply. They have no hysteresis, so the circuit around them must guard against false triggering near threshold. From either control input to the output transistors the response time is 400 ns with 100 mV overdrive, giving control within half a cycle up to 300 kHz.

The PWM comparator sets pulse width by comparing the CT ramp with the error-amplifier output. A series diode sits in the CT path but not in the control path, so the control voltage must be about 0.7 V above CT to stop the output; maximum duty cycle therefore needs no pull to true ground. As the amplifier output goes from 0.5 V to 3.5 V the pulse width falls from 97 % of the period to zero.

Both amplifiers are high-gain, single-supply types biased from the supply rail, with a common-mode range of -0.3 V to 2 V below it. Their outputs can only pull up, and they are ORed on FEEDBACK, so whichever asks for the narrower pulse wins. A current sink pulls FEEDBACK low (0.7 mA), giving full pulse width when both amplifiers are off.

OUTPUT CTRL supplies the pulse-steering flip-flop and acts directly on the outputs, regardless of the oscillator or flip-flop; it is meant to be fixed by the application. Grounded, it disables the flip-flop and both transistors carry the same pulses together (single-ended or parallel). Tied to REF, the flip-flop enables the two transistors alternately (push-pull). The logic never lets one output pulse twice in a row in push-pull.

Two uncommitted MOSFET outputs with drain and source both brought out, usable common-source or source-follower, each sinking or sourcing up to 200 mA. Saturation is under 1.3 V common-source and under 2.5 V source-follower. They are protected against excess dissipation but do not limit current enough to work as current-source outputs.

In the example, C2 runs from REF to DTC and R6 from DTC to ground. At power-up C2 holds DTC at 5 V, so the outputs are off (100 % dead time); as C2 charges through R6 the pulses widen until the loop takes over. R7 from REF and R6 (about 10:1) leave 0.5 V on DTC afterwards. Soft start lowers the switch stress from the surge into the output capacitor and helps reject false signals while the control circuit powers up.

Error amplifier 2 limits load current in the example: R1 and R2 put about 1 V on its inverting input, and R13 in series with the load brings its non-inverting input to 1 V at 10 A, after which the pulses shorten.

R3 and R4 halve the 5 V reference to 2.5 V, and R8 and R9 halve the output to compare against it. RF from FEEDBACK to the inverting input sets the closed-loop amplifier gain to about 101 for stability.

The part runs from 7 V to 40 V, which should be well regulated. If the source is more than a few inches away, bulk capacitance can be needed beside the ceramic bypass capacitors; 47 µF tantalum is a usual choice, depending on output power.

Prefer a low-EMI inductor with a closed ferrite core (toroid or encased E core); an open core needs low EMI, more distance from low-power parts and its poles perpendicular to the board, and stick cores radiate most. Route feedback short, fairly wide and away from the inductor and power traces, best on the opposite side with a ground plane between; distance from noise matters more than shortness. Place a small ceramic input capacitor right at VCC, any feed-forward capacitor from output to feedback close to the IC, and compensation parts close to the IC but not near the inductor; surface-mount parts reduce lead length. Make power traces short, direct and at least 15 mils (0.381 mm) wide per ampere. Keep inductor, output capacitors and output diode close together. Join the grounds of the IC, input and output capacitors and diode straight to a ground plane, with planes on both sides. On boards of more than two layers, put a ground plane between the power layer and the signal layer. Use one standard via per 200 mA when current must change layer. Arrange the parts so the switch-on and switch-off current loops circulate the same way, which avoids field reversal and cuts radiated EMI.

A PNP NTE153 driving an NPN NTE331 forms a hybrid Darlington that must saturate at IO + ΔIL/2, about 10.8 A, while its gain keeps the TL494 output current under its 250 mA limit; the base drive works out to 144 mA.
